clue.text: Mincing Lane gang annoyed with Eleanor's memorial

parts.note: Mincing Lane in the City of London was the centre of the British tea trade, so it stands for CHA, slang for tea
a ring is a gang, as in a spy ring or drugs ring
cross means annoyed or angry

explanation.surface: A gang from a City street, angry about a monument to a queen called Eleanor.
explanation.walkthrough: MINCING LANE, a London street, was where tea was traded, giving CHA. Edward I raised crosses where Queen Eleanor's coffin rested overnight; the last stood at CHARING CROSS, now a London station.
explanation.definitionFit: Charing Cross takes its name from the last of the stone crosses Edward I put up in memory of his queen, Eleanor of Castile.

clue.text: Was the first one floated by Adam and Eve, and wrecked by Cain?

definitions.text: Was the first one floated by Adam and Eve, and wrecked by Cain?

parts.words: Was the first one floated by Adam and Eve, and wrecked by Cain
parts.note: reads like a business launched by the first couple and ruined by their son; the saying that two makes a pleasant group but three a crowd explains it

explanation.surface: Biblical history recast as the story of the first business, launched by Adam and Eve and ruined by Cain.
explanation.walkthrough: The saying is 'Two's company, three's a crowd': Adam and Eve made company, and Cain's arrival made a crowd. 'Floated' and 'wrecked' make it sound like a firm.
explanation.definitionFit: A company is a business floated on the market and also the companionship of two people together.

clue.text: Melody-notes of "Come fly with me"?

parts.note: an air is a tune or melody
a line is a short letter, as in 'drop me a line', so notes can mean a line

explanation.surface: Asking what musical notes make up the song 'Come Fly with Me'.
explanation.walkthrough: The song title doubles as an invitation an air carrier might make in its advertising.
explanation.definitionFit: An invitation to fly with someone is what a passenger carrier's advertising says.

clue.text: That Latin bilge terrible, can't read it

parts.note: ille is the Latin word for 'that'

indicators.note: terrible signals that the letters of the word bilge are put into a disordered state

explanation.surface: A complaint that some Latin is rubbish and impossible to make out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' turns BILGE into GIBLE, after ILLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Writing too messy to decipher is said to be impossible to make out.

clue.text: Theatre cat's eaten two quarters at a surmise

indicators.note: eaten means the cat has swallowed the other letters, so they sit inside his name

parts.note: Gus is the Theatre Cat in T. S. Eliot's Old Possum's Book of Practical Cats
E and S are two compass quarters, east and south

explanation.surface: A theatre cat swallowing two quarters of something is offered as a supposition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eaten' puts ES inside GUS. 'at a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To surmise is to suppose without proof, which is what a guess is.

clue.text: King emperor holds a musical instrument of course

indicators.note: holds means the royal title contains the other pieces

parts.note: RI stands for Rex Imperator, Latin for king and emperor
the viol is an early bowed string instrument

explanation.surface: A royal ruler keeping a stringed instrument, apparently as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: RI, from Rex Imperator, is found on old British coins. 'of course' is the definition: a dish served as a course of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta parcels are a dish served as one course of a meal.

clue.text: One in a suit has this vest on

indicators.note: has signals that the bridge term is this word plus the word on, so on is taken away to leave it

parts.note: a singleton is a lone card held in a suit at bridge
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone in a suit is wearing a vest beneath it.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'a singleton (One in a suit) has this, vest, on': take ON from SINGLETON to leave the vest.
explanation.definitionFit: A singlet is a sleeveless undershirt, which British English calls a vest.

clue.text: Where young German pupils await Maud?

definitions.text: Where young German pupils await Maud?

parts.words: Where young German pupils await Maud
parts.note: German Kinder are children, and Tennyson's line 'Come into the garden, Maud' supplies where they wait

explanation.surface: German schoolchildren waiting for someone called Maud.
explanation.walkthrough: The German for children plus Tennyson's 'Come into the garden, Maud' builds the nursery school, whose German name means children's garden.
explanation.definitionFit: A nursery school for very young children takes its name from the German for children's garden.

clue.text: I am head of a monastery — or a novice without principles

parts.note: I am shortens to I'm

indicators.note: head of picks the opening letter of the word monastery

parts.note: taken as written
L, for learner, stands for a novice, as on L-plates

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether they are an abbot or a novice monk.
explanation.walkthrough: L-plates mark a learner driver in Britain, so L is a novice.
explanation.definitionFit: Having no principles means lacking any moral standards.

clue.text: Poison-even disguised with a French name

indicators.note: disguised says the letters of even are put into another form

parts.note: nom is French for name

explanation.surface: A poison passed off with a French label.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disguised' turns EVEN into ENVE; 'with' joins it to NOM.
explanation.definitionFit: To envenom is to put venom into something, that is, to poison it.

clue.text: His territory invaded by a small stepper and giant leaper

definitions.text: His territory invaded by a small stepper and giant leaper

parts.words: His territory invaded by a small stepper and giant leaper
parts.note: recalls Neil Armstrong's words on the lunar surface about one small step and one giant leap

explanation.surface: Someone's land is overrun by a tiny walker and a huge jumper.
explanation.walkthrough: Armstrong's 1969 line was 'one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind'; the face seen on the lunar disc saw his home invaded.
explanation.definitionFit: The face folklore sees on the lunar disc belongs to a figure whose home the 1969 astronauts visited.

clue.text: Pen-portrait of the flying doctor?

parts.note: a-wing is an old word meaning in flight, on the wing

explanation.surface: A written sketch of a doctor who flies to patients, as in the Australian outback.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pen-portrait' suggests a written description, but a sketch done with a pen is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A sketch done with a pen is a picture made by hand.

clue.text: Sell now if troubled with inflation

indicators.note: troubled signals that the letters of sell now are stirred up into a new order

explanation.surface: Advice to sell up if worried about rising prices.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troubled' rearranges SELL NOW. 'if' is a link. 'inflation' sounds economic but means puffing up.
explanation.definitionFit: Something puffed up or enlarged by inflation has grown bigger.

clue.text: Poe's runic poetry

parts.note: refers to Poe's poem The Bells, which has 'keeping time, time, time, in a sort of Runic' verse

explanation.surface: A note on the strange, rune-like poems of Edgar Allan Poe.
explanation.walkthrough: Poe's The Bells contains the line 'Keeping time, time, time, In a sort of Runic rhyme'.
explanation.definitionFit: Verse whose lines end in matching sounds is the poetry Poe calls runic in The Bells.

clue.text: Feathers flying? What a game!

parts.note: a squabble with feathers flying looks like a fight, but the feathers are on a shuttlecock hit over a net

explanation.surface: An exclamation about a scrap so fierce feathers are flying.
explanation.walkthrough: The game is played with a feathered shuttlecock, so feathers really do fly.
explanation.definitionFit: A racket sport played with a feathered shuttlecock sends feathers across the net.

clue.text: Paper said, oddly enough, to copy the Cheshire Cat

indicators.note: oddly enough signals that the letters of paper said are set out in a strange new order

explanation.surface: A newspaper reports something odd about imitating Lewis Carroll's grinning cat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly enough' rearranges PAPER SAID. In Alice in Wonderland the Cheshire Cat fades away until only its grin is left.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cheshire Cat famously vanishes, leaving only its grin, so copying it means vanishing.

clue.text: Their beastly motto "Down with the workers!"

definitions.text: Their beastly motto "Down with the workers!"

parts.words: Their beastly motto "Down with the workers
parts.note: sounds like a revolutionary slogan, but the workers are worker insects swallowed by animals

explanation.surface: A political slogan against the working class, chanted by some beastly group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down with' reads as a protest cry but means swallowed: these animals gulp down worker ants.
explanation.definitionFit: Animals that live on a diet of ants swallow the worker insects down.

clue.text: Hot air from the old shop, over money

annotationWithheld.why: Hot air from the old shop, over money: THE plus an old shop over L for money should give THERMAL, but no word for shop gives RMA; the parse cannot be completed
annotationWithheld.clue: Hot air from the old shop, over money

clue.text: Such rays are troublesome in cacti

indicators.note: troublesome signals that the letters of in cacti are thrown into disorder

explanation.surface: Some rays cause trouble for cactus plants.
explanation.walkthrough: 'troublesome' rearranges IN CACTI; 'are' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Actinic rays are light able to cause chemical change, like the ultraviolet that harms plants.

clue.text: The Tragic Muse has returned without the artist…

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside means the reversed word goes round the other piece
returned means the word has is read the other way round

parts.note: taken as written
RA, Royal Academician, is the crossword's standard artist

explanation.surface: A muse of tragedy comes back without the painter who portrayed her.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' gives SAH, and 'without' (outside) puts it round RA. Reynolds painted the actress Mrs Siddons as The Tragic Muse.
explanation.definitionFit: Reynolds' portrait Mrs Siddons as the Tragic Muse shows the actress Sarah Siddons.

clue.text: So prepare pencils, puzzlers, and wits

definitions.text: So prepare pencils, puzzlers, and wits

parts.words: So prepare pencils, puzzlers, and wits
parts.note: an instruction to solvers to put a point on both their pencils and their minds

explanation.surface: Advice to crossword solvers to get ready with pencils and clear heads.
explanation.walkthrough: One verb fits both pencils and wits: give each a keener point.
explanation.definitionFit: To give a pencil a point, or a mind an edge, is to make each keener.

clue.text: Quick takings for small profiteers?

parts.note: alludes to the shopkeeper's motto small profits and quick takings back

explanation.surface: The fast income that petty traders aim for.
explanation.walkthrough: The trader's motto is 'Small profits, quick returns': the quick takings are what comes back.
explanation.definitionFit: Returns are money coming back from trade, the takings in the motto 'Small profits, quick returns'.

clue.text: … to evoke the anguished tear here?

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: anguished signals that the letters of tear are twisted out of shape

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, a place where tears of anguish are drawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'anguished' turns TEAR into ATRE after THE. 'to evoke' is link words, and the dots join it to the clue before.
explanation.definitionFit: A playhouse is the place where tragedy draws tears from an audience.

clue.text: No odds what one does with a plane

definitions.meaning: in betting, even money means the stakes are matched with no favourable odds

definitions.text: what one does with a plane
definitions.meaning: a carpenter's plane levels and smooths wood

explanation.surface: Whatever one does with an aeroplane, it makes no difference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plane' looks like an aircraft but is the woodworker's tool.
explanation.definitionFit: Even-money odds pay stake for stake, and smoothing wood with a plane makes it level.

clue.text: Wordsworth's delightful ghost

definitions.meaning: Wordsworth's poem begins 'She was a ... of delight'

explanation.surface: A ghost that the poet Wordsworth found delightful.
explanation.walkthrough: Wordsworth's poem opens 'She was a Phantom of delight'.
explanation.definitionFit: Wordsworth calls a woman a vision of delight, and a spectre is an apparition.

clue.text: Man proposed one amendment about fuel source:

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the other piece
an amendment changes something, so the letters of one are altered in order

parts.note: a coal mine is a source of fuel

explanation.surface: Someone proposes an amendment to a motion about where fuel comes from.
explanation.walkthrough: 'amendment' turns ONE into NOE, and 'about' puts it round MINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone put forward as a candidate for a post is a person proposed for it.

clue.text: Tap with rose needed to produce grass

indicators.note: to produce suggests making something new out of the letters of tap and rose by reordering them

explanation.surface: A tap fitted with a watering rose is needed to grow grass.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rose' looks like the flower, or a sprinkler head, but it is just letters. 'with' and 'needed' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Esparto is a tough Spanish and North African grass used for paper and rope.

clue.text: Miss Liddell appears jumpy in Australia

parts.note: Alice Liddell was the girl who inspired Lewis Carroll's Alice
springs means jumps or bounds

explanation.surface: The original Alice of Wonderland seems nervous while visiting Australia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appears jumpy' is a verb phrase for leaps. 'in Australia' defines a place found there.
explanation.definitionFit: Alice Springs is a town in the Northern Territory of Australia.
